<reflection>
- The first experiment resulted in very similar Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) values across all 20 mechanisms (ranging from -22.59 to -25.48). This indicates that a standard kinetic profile (S=2.0, cat=0.05, P=0.0) lacks the specific features required to differentiate the models, as most mechanisms can adjust their rate constants to fit a simple saturation curve.
- My aim to establish a baseline was achieved, but it confirms that we must now actively perturb the system to break the degeneracy. We need to introduce conditions that trigger higher-order catalyst effects and product-dependent pathways.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To break the current degeneracy, we must introduce experimental conditions that force the mechanisms to diverge in their predictions. 
1. By adding a high initial concentration of product (P=0.5), we will strongly differentiate mechanisms involving product inhibition or product-induced deactivation (M5, M12, M17) from those that are insensitive to product.
2. By significantly increasing the catalyst concentration to its maximum allowed value (cat=0.20), we will test the linearity of the reaction rate with respect to the catalyst. This will isolate mechanisms with second-order catalyst interactions, such as dimerization (M2, M3) or bimolecular deactivation (M13, M18, M19).
3. Using a moderate substrate concentration (S=1.0) ensures a balance between free catalyst and substrate-bound catalyst (catS). This allows both free-catalyst-dependent pathways (e.g., M12, M13) and catS-dependent pathways (e.g., M17, M18) to be active and observable. 
This combination of high product and high catalyst is expected to cause massive divergence in the fitting quality of the currently tied models.
</hypothesis>
